mappings.note: Where impurity/metal deposits during electrolytic refining of copper. Refining is the last step of the extraction outcome LO-6; no corrosion or reactivity is involved.

Soft, air-sensitive, vigorous with water -> sodium. The deciding evidence is the violence of the water reaction, i.e. position at the top of the reactivity series (LO-2), not the knife-softness alone.
Which alloy has a non-metal constituent (steel, carbon). Alloy composition; LO-7 is the only outcome that names alloying.
Picks the false statement about magnesium with cold water / hot water / steam. Graded water reactivity, LO-2.
Which alloy contains mercury (zinc amalgam). Alloy composition, LO-7.
X loses and Y gains electrons, so Z is ionic; picks the property it does NOT have. Ionic compound formation and its consequences sit at the C 1.1 competency -- no LO covers bonding.
Decides which of X (2,8), Y (2,8,6), Z (2,8,1) are metals. The verdict asked for is exactly LO-1's classification, although the evidence here is electron configuration rather than a bench property.
Which metal gives an amphoteric rather than basic oxide (Zn). Nature of the oxide is the chemical property LO-1 classifies on.
The non-metal that conducts (graphite) -- an exception to the physical-property rule in LO-1.
Insulating coating on electrical wire (PVC). Tests the conductivity contrast that LO-1 classifies on; nothing in the frame is closer.
The liquid non-metal (bromine). Physical state, LO-1.
Which metal/salt pair reacts (CuSO4 + Al). Prediction of displacement from the reactivity series, LO-2.

Picks the correct electrolytic-refining diagram. The figure options are not printed by the tool, but the stem itself names the process, so the outcome is determined even though the key is not checkable here.

A divalent metal giving hydrogen with BOTH NaOH and HCl -> zinc, i.e. amphoteric behaviour. Cited to LO-1 (chemical-property classification) rather than LO-2, because the reaction with alkali, not acid, is what identifies it.
Anode, cathode, electrolyte and where pure copper collects. Refining step of LO-6.
Why sulphide and carbonate ores are first turned into oxides -- roasting/calcination before reduction, squarely LO-6.
Why nitric acid does not liberate hydrogen. The rule it is an exception to (metal displaces hydrogen from acid) is LO-2.
Thermite welding of rails: Fe2O3 + Al. Aluminium displaces iron because it is higher in the series -- LO-2. Not LO-6: this is a field repair, not ore-to-metal extraction.
Metal giving XOH of mass 56 with COLD water plus a flammable gas -> potassium. Identification rests on cold-water reactivity, LO-2.
Carbon with diamond (hardest) and graphite (conducting). Physical properties of a non-metal and its exceptions, LO-1.
Al + MnO2: which species is reduced and which oxidised. The reaction happens because Al outranks Mn, so LO-2; the redox bookkeeping has no separate outcome in this frame.
Composition of solder and the low melting point that suits it to wiring. Alloy property, LO-7.
Aluminium's oxide is amphoteric; write its reactions with HCl and NaOH. The demand is oxide nature (LO-1); the thermite mention is only a clue to the identity.
Mercury from cinnabar by heating the sulphide in air. Extraction of a low-reactivity metal, LO-6.
Formulae of binary compounds from Ca/N, Li/O, Ca/Cl. Pure valency work, which the C 1.1 competency names; neither LO covers writing formulae.
Calcination of ZnCO3 and the self-reduction of Cu2O with Cu2S. Both are extraction steps, LO-6.
Carbon identified from its two oxides (CO toxic, CO2 a greenhouse gas): non-metal oxide behaviour is LO-1, and the follow-up asking for its Periodic Table group is the classification clause of C 1.1.
Examples of metals that conduct heat well and poorly. Physical-property classification, LO-1.
A liquid metal and a liquid non-metal, plus low-melting metals. Physical state and melting point, LO-1.
Calcium with water giving slaked lime, then CaO and back. The identification hinges on a metal reacting with water, LO-2, not on extraction or corrosion.
Alkali metal + water -> KOH (mass 56) is LO-2; the second step, KOH dissolving Al2O3, only works because that oxide is amphoteric, which is LO-1.
A metal that will not liberate hydrogen from acid but blackens with oxygen -> copper. The discriminating fact is its position below hydrogen in the series, LO-2.
An acidic A2O3 means A is a non-metal. Oxide nature used to classify, LO-1.
Holes in an iron pot holding CuSO4, explained in terms of reactivity, with the equation. The stem asks for reactivity, so LO-2 rather than the corrosion outcome LO-7.
Nitrogen identified via NH3, its oxide and HNO3: non-metal and its oxide chemistry is LO-1, and the group-placement part is the Periodic Table clause of C 1.1.
Steps for extracting low- and medium-reactivity metals from sulphide ores. This is LO-6 restated.

Five unrelated parts: (b) carbon cannot reduce Na/Mg oxides and (e) these metals are never free -> LO-6; (d) galvanising -> LO-7; (c) NaCl conductivity -> the ionic-bonding competency C 1.1. Part (a), aluminium passivated by conc. HNO3, also touches LO-2 but the three-code cap leaves it out; it is the smallest part.
Roasting, reduction and electrolytic refining of copper with a labelled cell diagram. The full extraction chain, LO-6.
X reacts with cold water, Y with hot, Z only with steam; name them and order them. Reactivity ordering, LO-2.
A carbonate ore and a sulphide ore: which steps turn each into the metal. Calcination vs roasting then reduction, LO-6.
24-carat versus 22-carat gold and why pure gold is too soft to work. Alloying to change a metal's properties, LO-7.

Impure copper wrongly wired as cathode in a refining cell; what the mistake was and the electrode reaction. Refining step of LO-6. C 8.2 was considered but its only LO is about comparing two metals' reactivity, which this is not.
Most abundant metal in the crust (aluminium). Occurrence of metals, the starting point of LO-6.
Calcination versus roasting. Both are ore-to-oxide steps in LO-6.
Formula of rust. Corrosion, LO-7.
Froth flotation for enriching sulphide ore -- concentration step of LO-6.
Zinc or iron: which gives hydrogen with dilute HCl more readily. A direct two-metal reactivity comparison, LO-2.
Brass versus bronze composition. Alloy composition, LO-7.
Whether german silver contains silver. Alloy composition, LO-7.
Formulae of the chief ores of iron and aluminium. Ores, LO-6.
The conducting non-metal (graphite). Physical-property exception, LO-1.
Two neutral oxides (CO, N2O). Nature of non-metal oxides, LO-1.
Formulae of zinc blende and galena -- ores, LO-6. (Note the question is tagged 'Chemical Reactivity of Metals' in the bank, which is wrong.)
Examples by melting point and by conductivity, including a conducting non-metal. Physical-property classification, LO-1.
What serves as anode in electro-refining (the impure metal). Refining step of LO-6.
Names the bond between a metal and a non-metal (ionic). Bond formation from atomic structure -- the C 1.1 competency; no LO reaches bonding.
Why salts melt high -- the electrostatic lattice from electron transfer. Same competency as the other ionic-property items; C 1.2 covers mixtures and separations instead.
Two metals found native. Occurrence of unreactive metals, LO-6.
MnO2 heated with aluminium powder -- an aluminothermic displacement, predicted from relative reactivity. LO-2, same reading as the other thermite items.
Whether an iron nail rusts in distilled water. Conditions required for corrosion, LO-7.
